title: The divine dance
hook: Greek fathers described the three persons as dwelling in one another, like a round dance

segments.voice: Yesterday, the filioque: and the Son, said in the creed in the West, not the East. Your line was one word, long argument.

A circle of people at a wedding, arms on each other's shoulders, stepping left, then right. Nobody in the circle is the center. Nobody leads for long. If one person stops, the whole ring feels it. And if you ask where the dance is, you can't point to any one dancer. It's in all of them, and between them. Some Christian writers have reached for exactly that picture to talk about God. Not a ruler on a throne, not a triangle on a whiteboard: a ring of movement. Like every picture of the Trinity, it falls short, but in a lively way.

Perichoresis. Greek Christian writers used it for something Jesus says in John's Gospel. He asks Philip: "Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me?" Not beside. In. Later, praying for his friends, he widens it: "as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us." Teachers in the Greek-speaking churches, John of Damascus among them, used perichoresis to name that mutual in-ness: Father, Son and Spirit each dwelling in the others, without blurring into one another and without being split apart. Each makes room for the others, and is at home in them. Now the dance. In English the word sounds like choreography, and some modern writers have run with that: God as a round dance, three persons moving in one movement. Others point out that the root is about going around and making room, not dancing, and would rather keep the picture loose. Both agree on what it's for. God is not a lonely thing. Before there was anything, Christians say, there was already giving and receiving, love going out and coming back. And then the prayer: that they also may be one in us. The circle has a gap, and the gap is held open. Christians differ on how far to push that. Orthodox teachers speak boldly of people being drawn into God's life; others put it more carefully. Either way, the ring in this picture is not closed.
screen: `I IN THE FATHER, THE FATHER IN ME.`
`A RING WITH A GAP HELD OPEN.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and turn slowly all the way around, a full breath for each step; if not, trace a slow circle with one hand. As you turn, think of the people who make room for you, and the people you make room for. If you pray, say the line from John, that they also may be one in us; if not, let the circle be the whole of it.
Perichoresis. The persons of the Trinity dwelling in one another, each making room for the others: some say, like a dance.
Your line: god is a dance. A ring, with a gap held open. Go gently.

howItsDone: Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant theologians use the word perichoresis when they teach about the Trinity, and some churches have icons and hymns that speak of the three persons dwelling in one another.

chat.says: What does it mean when Christians picture God as a kind of dance?
options: Father, Son and Spirit dwell in one another, each making room: love given and returned.
It means God is three separate dancers who take turns leading the world.
It means God was lonely before creation, so made people to dance with.
chat.meaning: Perichoresis names Father, Son and Spirit each dwelling in the others, making room, never blurred or split. God is not a lonely thing.

notes: The index hook says 'like a round dance'. Perichoresis is usually derived from perichoreo (to go around, to make room), not choreuo (to dance); the dance picture is a popular modern association. The script presents both views without stating an etymology as fact. Confirm wording.
John of Damascus named as one Greek teacher who used perichoresis of the Trinity (Exposition 1.8, 1.14); confirm the chapter references.
'Orthodox teachers speak boldly of people being drawn into God's life' points toward theosis; confirm it is fair, and that 'others put it more carefully' does not rank anyone.
'Last week's pictures of the Trinity' refers to day 1070 (Pictures of the Trinity), which falls in the previous week (days 1065–1071). Confirm.
Practice invites a slow turn in a circle, with a hand-tracing alternative for anyone who can't stand.
